Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120) (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): Lingao Benyu is the exact headword speaker. Lingao Benyu owns the exact clause in the complete case.

Senses.Explanation: An instant is a very short interval. Yongzheng Emperor says that it is swift as a finger-snap. Wuyi Yuanlai compares three elapsed years to the interval of an instant, while Zhongfeng Mingben says there is no instant without birth and change or cessation. Yongming Yanshou uses flowing water to describe the previous instant ceasing and the next arising. Chijue Daochong gives a finer inherited reckoning whose source-visible count reads literally ‘six-thousand-five’ instants in one finger-snap, followed by 900 arisings and cessations in one instant; no parallel or apparatus variant resolves whether the first written number is meant as 6,005, a colloquially shortened 6,500, or a textual error. Lingao Benyu instead begins from one thought containing ninety instants and likewise gives 900 arisings and cessations within each instant. Those differently framed calculations confirm extreme brevity but do not establish a single modern duration. Yang Jie says the Source-Mirror's treasure is gained without even an instant's exertion. Ziyang Zhenren contrasts becoming buddha in an instant with wandering for myriad ages. These named speakers repeatedly bend the tiny time-unit into a sharp interval for change, attainment, or contrast, without turning the interval into a person, title, or separate lexical object.

Senses.Explanation: Li Ao is the Tang official whom Zen records place in exchanges with Yaoshan and other masters. Records identify Li Ao as an official who questions masters and appears most prominently in exchanges with Xitang Zhizang and Yaoshan Weiyan. In the Xitang encounter he asks what Mazu taught; Xitang calls his name, Li answers, and Xitang says the drums and horns have sounded. Multiple lamp records preserve that same encounter and are one case family. Zen defines this dictionary identity through the questions, responses, and later citations in which he is deployed, not through an outside literary biography.

Senses.Explanation: Raising one finger is the defining response-action of the Juzhi case and a target of later appraisal. Records recount, list, imitate, praise, and criticize the gesture precisely because it was made in answer to public questions. A lamp record mocks old Juzhi for ‘groundlessly raising one finger.’ Other commentaries list the gesture beside Luzu's wall-facing, Shigong's bow, and Mimo's fork as a recognizable response-action. Yuanwu and Mingben warn that imitating such visible acts can trap a student in a borrowed form. The gesture is therefore both transported as Juzhi's answer and criticized when copied as performance.

Senses.Explanation: To raise upright is a narrated physical action applied to a fist, staff, or whisk before a question or response. The records narrate Tianyi Ruzhe raising his fist before asking where it falls, Tianyin Yuanxiu raising a staff before testing recognition, Baichi Yuan raising a whisk and asking whether it is seen, Songyuan Chongyue raising a whisk in answer to what is transmitted, Baizhang Huaihai raising Mazu's whisk, Yuansou Xingduan raising a whisk and calling it the teaching, and Xiangya Ting raising a staff before a statement about one speck.

Senses.Explanation: The seven awakened ones of the past are the inherited group whom Zen records place inside transmission formulas and public cases. The records invoke their ritual form, transmission of precepts, and inclusion in a bag that silences ancient and future figures alike.
